reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: MPGN is a histological pattern of mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity with capillary wall remodelling, not a single disease
Light microscopy shows a lobular glomerular architecture with double-contour ('tram-track') basement membranes from subendothelial deposits and mesangial interposition
Modern classification is based on immunofluorescence: immune-complex/immunoglobulin-mediated MPGN versus complement-mediated C3 glomerulopathy (C3 glomerulonephritis and dense deposit disease)
Immunoglobulin-positive patterns point to infection, autoimmune disease or a monoclonal gammopathy, so a paraprotein screen is essential in adults
C3-dominant staining with scanty immunoglobulin indicates dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, sometimes with C3 nephritic factor or complement gene abnormalities
Clinical presentation spans nephrotic syndrome, nephritic features with haematuria, or a mixed picture, frequently with persistently low serum complement
Treatment targets the underlying cause: eradicate infection, treat autoimmune disease or the paraprotein-producing clone, and consider complement-directed therapy in refractory C3 glomerulopathy
reference.pathophysiology: The MPGN pattern results from deposition of immune complexes or complement components in the mesangium and subendothelial space, which activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells. Mesangial cells proliferate and interpose their cytoplasm between the endothelium and the glomerular basement membrane while laying down new basement membrane material, producing the characteristic double-contour appearance. In immune-complex disease the trigger is chronic antigenaemia from infection, autoimmunity or a monoclonal immunoglobulin; in C3 glomerulopathy uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, from acquired autoantibodies (such as C3 nephritic factor) or inherited regulator defects, drives predominant C3 deposition, with dense osmiophilic transformation of the basement membrane in dense deposit disease.
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to separate immune-complex from complement-mediated disease
Serum C3 and C4 with an alternative-pathway complement assessment
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains to detect a paraprotein
Autoimmune serology including antinuclear and anti-DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins
Complement functional assays, C3 nephritic factor and complement regulator/gene testing in C3 glomerulopathy
Screening for chronic infection where an immune-complex pattern is found
redFlags: Crescentic transformation with rapidly progressive renal impairment
Persistently low complement with systemic features suggesting active autoimmune or cryoglobulinaemic disease
Detection of a monoclonal protein indicating an underlying haematological clone
reference.prognosis: The MPGN pattern is often chronic and progressive, with a substantial proportion reaching end-stage kidney disease, though outcome is strongly influenced by the underlying cause and its treatment. Dense deposit disease and crescentic forms carry a poorer prognosis, and both immune-complex and complement-mediated disease can recur after transplantation.
pitfalls: Treating the pattern as a single entity instead of pursuing the immune-complex versus complement cause
Failing to screen adults for a monoclonal gammopathy driving the disease
Overlooking chronic infection as a reversible trigger
Assuming normal complement excludes the diagnosis
Giving broad immunosuppression in complement-mediated disease without addressing the pathway dysregulation
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, whether chronic infection, autoimmune disease or a monoclonal gammopathy in immune-complex disease
Use renin-angiotensin system blockade with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker to reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure
Give immunosuppression such as corticosteroids with mycophenolate or a calcineurin inhibitor for idiopathic immune-complex disease with heavy proteinuria or declining function
Consider complement inhibition with a terminal complement C5 inhibitor such as eculizumab for progressive C3 glomerulopathy
Direct clone-targeted therapy where a monoclonal immunoglobulin is driving the disease
Provide general nephroprotection with lipid control, oedema management and dietary sodium restriction
Consider transplantation with counselling on the risk of disease recurrence in the graft
